question: Tell me about yourself.
outline: Present tense opener: course, college, and the one line about what you build or enjoy most.
One proof point: your strongest project or internship and the outcome in numbers (users, accuracy, load time).
Skills that map to the role — 2-3 specific technologies, not adjectives.
Close forward: why this company/role is the logical next step for you.
Keep it 60-90 seconds; rehearse until it sounds spoken, not memorised.

question: Walk me through a project you are proud of. What was your specific contribution?
outline: Set context in one sentence: what the project does and who it is for — Resist a full feature tour.
Your role: what YOU personally designed, built, or debugged (use 'I', not 'we').
The hard part: one technical obstacle and how you solved it.
Result with a number: benchmarks, users, deployment, grade — anything measurable.
What you would do differently — shows engineering judgment.

question: Describe a time you had a conflict or disagreement in a team. How did you handle it?
outline: Name the disagreement concretely (tech choice, workload split, deadline) without blaming.
Your move: you listened first, then argued with data or a working prototype, not volume.
The resolution and what it cost — compromise is fine to admit.
The outcome and the relationship after: did you ship, and would that teammate work with you again?
Red flag to avoid: stories where you were always right.

question: Tell me about a failure or a mistake that cost you something. What did you change after it?
outline: Pick a real failure — a bad grade, a missed deadline, a bug that reached users — not a humble-brag.
Own it in one sentence: what YOU did or didn't do.
The lesson stated as a changed behaviour, not a vague feeling.
Proof the change stuck: the next time you applied the fix and what improved.
Tone: matter-of-fact, no drama, no excuses.

question: Give an example of when you led without formal authority.
outline: Frame the gap: something needed doing and nobody was assigned to do it.
Your specific action: you split the work, set a checkpoint, or unblocked a teammate.
How you brought peers along — influence, not instruction.
Concrete result: delivered on time, quality bar met, or someone else then repeated the pattern.
This is how they test whether 'team lead' on your resume is real.

question: Why should we hire you over other candidates?
outline: Restate their need first: what the role actually requires (from the JD) — proves you read it.
Match #1: your strongest technical fit with one line of evidence.
Match #2: a differentiator — shipped project, open-source, or speed of learning shown by example.
Culture/attitude fit: reliability and how you work in a team, one sentence.
Close with confidence, not arrogance: 'I can start contributing from week one because…'

question: Explain the four pillars of object-oriented programming with one concrete example for each.
outline: Encapsulation: bundle data + methods, restrict state via private fields and accessors (BankAccount.balance).
Abstraction: expose what, hide how — an interface like PaymentGateway with Stripe/UPI implementations.
Inheritance: reuse behaviour through an is-a relation (Animal → Dog), and note its cost: tight coupling.
Polymorphism: same call, different behaviour at runtime (shape.area() on Circle vs Square).
Strong answers name where each pillar shows up in the code they have personally written.

question: Compare arrays and linked lists. When would you choose one over the other?
outline: Memory: arrays are contiguous; linked lists are nodes scattered with pointer overhead.
Access: array indexing O(1); linked list must walk O(n).
Insert/delete: middle of an array shifts O(n); linked list splices O(1) once you hold the node.
Cache reality: arrays win in practice because of CPU cache locality — interviewers love this nuance.
Choose arrays as the default; linked lists for queues/deques or when you splice mid-list constantly.

question: How would you detect a cycle in a linked list? Explain your approach and its complexity.
outline: Naive: visited set of node references — O(n) time, O(n) space; say it first to show you can start somewhere.
Better: Floyd's tortoise-and-hare — slow moves 1, fast moves 2; they meet inside the loop if one exists.
Why it works: inside a cycle the gap between pointers shrinks by 1 each step, so they must collide.
Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space — the reason this is the classic.
Bonus: to find WHERE the cycle starts, reset one pointer to head and walk both at speed 1 until they meet.

question: What is the difference between a process and a thread? What conditions cause a deadlock?
outline: Process: own address space, file descriptors, and heap — isolation; crash of one doesn't kill others.
Thread: lives inside a process, shares its heap and code but keeps its own stack and registers — cheap to create, communication is just shared memory.
Cost comparison: context switch between processes is heavier than between threads of the same process.
Deadlock needs all four Coffman conditions: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait.
Kill any one condition to prevent it — most common fix in practice: impose a global lock ordering.

question: What happens, end to end, when you type a URL into the browser and press Enter?
outline: DNS: browser cache → OS cache → resolver → root/TLD/authoritative — returns an IP.
TCP (and TLS): 3-way handshake opens the connection; TLS handshake negotiates keys for https.
HTTP request goes out; server (possibly via load balancer/CDN) responds with status + HTML.
Browser parse: DOM + CSSOM → render tree → layout → paint; JS may block parsing unless deferred.
Keep it layered and brief at each step — the interviewer picks one layer to drill into next.

question: Explain TCP vs UDP. Give a real application of each.
outline: TCP: connection-oriented, ordered, reliable, flow + congestion control — overhead in exchange for guarantees.
UDP: connectionless, no delivery/order promises, tiny header (8 bytes) — speed over safety.
TCP examples: web (HTTP/2, HTTPS), file transfer, email, databases.
UDP examples: video calls and gaming (stale frames are useless anyway), DNS lookups, QUIC/HTTP-3.
Nuance that lands: 'reliability' can be rebuilt at the application layer on top of UDP when you need custom control.

question: Explain database normalization up to 3NF. Why would you ever denormalize?
outline: 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups — one fact per cell, rows uniquely addressable.
2NF: 1NF + no partial dependency — non-key columns depend on the WHOLE composite key.
3NF: 2NF + no transitive dependency — non-key columns depend only on keys, 'the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key'.
Denormalize when read performance matters more: analytics tables, caching counts, feed timelines.
Trade-off framing: normalization protects writes/consistency; denormalization buys read speed by precomputing joins.

question: What are the ACID properties of transactions? Give an example where each matters.
outline: Atomicity: all or nothing — money transfer must debit AND credit or roll back both.
Consistency: constraints never violated — total balance stays constant across the transfer.
Isolation: concurrent transactions don't see each other's intermediate state — two users booking the last seat.
Durability: once committed, a power cut can't lose it — write-ahead logs before acknowledging.
Mention isolation levels (read committed, serializable) as the knob between correctness and throughput.

question: Explain time complexity of quicksort. When does its worst case occur, and how do you avoid it?
outline: Mechanics: pick a pivot, partition smaller/larger around it, recurse on both sides.
Average case: O(n log n) — balanced partitions halve the problem log n times, partitioning costs n.
Worst case: O(n²) — when every pivot lands on an extreme (e.g. sorted input with a first-element pivot), giving maximally lopsided partitions.
Avoidance: randomized pivot or median-of-three makes the bad input vanishingly unlikely.
Also worth saying: quicksort partitions in-place (low memory) while merge sort is stable but needs O(n) extra.

question: What is REST? What do the HTTP verbs and status codes actually mean?
outline: REST: resources addressed by URLs, manipulated through uniform HTTP verbs — stateless, cacheable requests.
GET reads (safe, no side effects), POST creates/triggers, PUT/PATCH updates, DELETE removes.
Status codes: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client's mistake (400 bad input, 401 not signed in, 403 forbidden, 404 missing, 429 rate-limited), 5xx server's fault.
401 vs 403 distinction trips people up: not authenticated vs authenticated but not allowed.
Tie to experience: 'in my project, DELETE /api/notes/:id returned 404 when the note wasn't mine.'

question: What are your greatest strengths and weaknesses?
outline: Strength: one real trait + one concrete proof (e.g., 'I debug systematically — I fixed a race condition by logging lock acquisition order').
Tie the strength to the role's daily work — relevance beats impressiveness.
Weakness: real but not fatal — never 'perfectionism' or 'I work too hard'.
Weakness arc: name it, show how you manage it, and show recent progress ('I over-prepared slides for weeks; now I timebox to one pass and one review').
Keep each half under 30 seconds — this question tests self-awareness, not vocabulary.

question: Are you willing to relocate, work night shifts, or sign a service bond if required?
outline: Answer directly first: yes / no / yes-with-conditions — HR wants clarity, not evasion.
If conditional, state the condition calmly (e.g., 'yes to relocation after my final semester').
Bond: ask what the commitment is before agreeing — duration and amount are legitimate questions.
Shifts: respond to the actual requirement; if it's rotational for the first year, saying yes is normal in service companies.
Never bluff hard no's to pass the round — you'll be held to it at offer stage.

question: Where do you see yourself in five years?
outline: Skill trajectory first: from executing assigned tickets to owning a module/system end to end.
Depth over titles: 'engineer the team trusts with the hard bug' beats 'team lead' — but mention leadership honestly if that's the goal.
Show the company in the picture: growing within THIS org, which signals you'll stay.
Avoid: 'your seat', 'CEO', or anything that sounds rehearsed or sarcastic.
Anchor on learning: specific domains you want to get good at (distributed systems, ML in production…).

question: Do you have any questions for us?
outline: Always have 2-3 ready — 'no questions' reads as disinterest.
Work reality: 'what does a typical first project for this team look like?'
Growth: 'how are juniors reviewed in the first six months?'
Team: 'what does the on-call or release rhythm look like?' (shows maturity).
Logistics questions (salary, timing) are fine for HR rounds but ask them last, courteously.

question: What is your expected salary, and on what basis?
outline: Anchor on the standard band for the role and the company tier — say you've looked at published campus packages.
Defer when early: 'I'd like to first understand the role's scope; I expect the standard band for this position.'
If forced to name a number: give a range with a clear floor you can justify by skill and benchmarks.
Justify with evidence: skills, projects, internships, market data — never personal needs.
Stay flexible on structure (fixed vs variable vs benefits) but firm on the floor.
